title: Day 32 · Week 4, Day 4 — Adventure: the trip that's already booked — flying in the first trimester, with the radiation in microsieverts and the clot risk with its baseline
summary: The first Adventure episode. Your baby is at Carnegie stage 8, 1–1.5 mm, and the neural plate has begun to dip into a neural groove — the first physical piece of the brain. Then the flight. ACOG, the CDC Yellow Book and the RCOG all say occasional air travel is safe in an uncomplicated pregnancy with ordinary precautions. The five questions in order of evidence: radiation (≈6 µSv/h at cruise; FAA route doses from 0.03 to 0.63 mSv per 100 block hours; a transatlantic round trip ≈ 70 µSv against a 1 mSv whole-pregnancy occupational limit for aircrew and a 100 mGy threshold below which no fetal effect is detectable); clots (pregnancy 4–5× baseline, 0.5–2 per 1,000; travel RR 2.8 with 26% per 2 h of flight; 1 event per 4,656 long-haul flights in 8,755 employees; compression stockings OR 0.10 in 12 RCTs, high certainty); oxygen (cabin ≈ 6,000–8,000 ft, saturation down ~10%, fetal heart rate normal in the only monitored study); miscarriage (no passenger study shows an increase; flight attendants flying a median 130 h a trimester had no more losses than teachers); and the one real veto, Zika at the destination, including the condom rule for a partner who travels. Airline rules start at 28 weeks and end at 36 (32 for twins), so for this trip there are none. Nausea, the seat belt, and the logistics that belong to the father.
action: Tonight, open the booking. Change her seat to an aisle. If any leg is over four hours, order graduated below-the-knee compression stockings (flight socks) in her size now, so they're in the house before you pack. Then look the destination up on the CDC's Zika travel page. If it's on the map, that's a conversation with her OB this week — the trip gets moved, not the pregnancy.
